Abstract  Fog computing has emerged as a pivotal 
paradigm for enabling low-latency, high-performance 
applications by positioning computational resources 
closer to the network edge. However, task offload-
ing in fog environments poses significant challenges 
because of the dynamic and heterogeneous nature 
of fog nodes, which are influenced by fluctuating 
computational loads, channel conditions, and mobil-
ity patterns. This paper introduces a dynamic task-
offloading framework leveraging deep Q-learning 
(DQL), a reinforcement learning technique tailored to 
optimize task allocation and enhance system perfor-
mance in such complex settings. The proposed frame-
work models the offloading problem as a Markov 
decision process (MDP), enabling the DQL agent to 
learn optimal strategies adaptively by incorporating 
factors such as task demands, node states, and chan-
nel quality. Performance evaluations against state-of-
the-art scheduling methods reveal that the DQL-based 
approach consistently outperforms competing tech-
niques, achieving superior efficiency and reliability. 
Furthermore, the framework demonstrates scalabil-
ity and robustness in dynamic fog networks, making 
it highly suitable for diverse real-time applications. 
This study highlights the potential of DQL as a trans-
formative solution for dynamic task offloading in fog 
computing, offering efficient resource management 
and system stability. Its applicability to domains such 
as intelligent transportation systems, smart cities, and 
the IoT underscores its practical relevance and future 
impact.

1  Introduction
As intelligent transportation systems (ITSs) have rap-
idly expanded and connected devices have become 
more common, the demand for computational power 
at network edges has increased substantially. These 
systems require real-time data processing and deci-
sion-making to keep things such as autonomous driv-
ing, traffic management, and vehicle-to-everything 
(V2X) communications running smoothly [1, 2]. 
Traditional cloud computing often falls short due 
to latency and bandwidth issues, primarily because 
cloud data centers are typically far from the devices 
they need to serve [3, 4].
This is where fog computing comes into play. Fog 
computing brings computing, storage, and networking 
resources closer to where the data are actually gener-
ated, such as at edge devices or roadside units (RSUs)

enables faster real-time decisions and alleviates the

enhances performance and flexibility but also contrib-
utes to safer and more efficient transportation systems

However, fog computing is not without its chal-
lenges. The environment is highly dynamic, with 
factors such as node mobility, wireless channel varia-
tions, and fluctuating computation loads at fog nodes 
making task offloading tricky [9, 10]. These unpre-
dictable elements make devising an offloading strat-
egy that can adapt quickly to the network difficult.
Research has explored various methods for task 
offloading, from heuristic-based approaches to 
cooperative computing strategies in fog environ-
ments. Heuristic methods typically use predefined 
rules or simplified models for offloading, whereas 
cooperative methods focus on resource sharing 
among multiple fog nodes [11, 12]. Despite these 
efforts, many strategies rely on static or semistatic 
models that do not fully capture the dynamic nature 
of fog environments, often leading to suboptimal 
resource use, longer task completion times, and 
potential bottlenecks at fog nodes [13, 14].
In this paper, we address these challenges with 
a dynamic task-offloading technique via deep 
Q-learning (DQL). DQL, a type of reinforcement 
learning, helps develop adaptive and intelligent sys-
tems that learn optimal strategies through continu-
ous interaction with their environment [15, 16]. By 
framing the task offloading problem as a Markov 
decision process (MDP), our DQL agent learns to 
make decisions that minimize task delay while bal-
ancing the computational load across fog nodes. 
The agent considers various factors, such as the 
current state of the fog nodes, task demands, and 
wireless channel quality, to make the best possible 
choices.

Fog computing plays a crucial role in task offload-
ing by providing an intermediary layer between edge 
devices and the cloud. While edge computing brings 
computations closer to end devices, it relies primarily 
on localized processing, which may be insufficient for 
resource-intensive applications. In contrast, fog com-
puting enables multinode coordination, distributed 
decision-making, and better load balancing, making it 
ideal for applications such as smart cities, the indus-
trial IoT, and real-time analytics.
Moreover, edge nodes typically have limited com-
putational power and may not efficiently handle mul-
tiple complex tasks. Fog computing alleviates this 
limitation by aggregating resources from multiple fog 
nodes, allowing for optimized resource allocation and 
improved system scalability. This hybrid approach 
minimizes latency while ensuring efficient resource 
utilization across diverse network conditions.

2  Related Work
In this section, we discuss recent progress in task 
offloading within fog computing environments, with 
a focus on AI-driven approaches and techniques for 
dynamic optimization. The study in [17] explored 
how fog computing can enhance task offloading for 
mobile devices. The authors propose a two-stage, 
online learning-based method. First, they allocate 
resources among fog nodes to reduce computational 
costs. Then, they fine-tune task allocation and spec-
trum scheduling to minimize offloading delays. This 
approach outperforms traditional upper confidence 
bound (UCB) techniques, showing that learning-
based methods can be highly effective for manag-
ing resources in fog computing. In [18], the authors 
address server engagement and task offloading via a 
convex-concave optimization strategy. Their frame-
work includes efficient server assignment and price-
matching solutions to reduce network delays. This 
approach addresses information asymmetry and 
uncertainty well, leading to better resource sharing 
and lower total delays.
The paper in [19] looks at task assignment and 
incentive mechanisms in fog computing through the 
lens of contract theory. It introduces a stable match-
ing algorithm for assigning tasks between fog nodes 
and devices, aiming to maximize overall utility. This 
work highlights how important incentive mechanisms 
and stable matching are for improving task offload-
ing efficiency. The research in [20] combines contract 
theory with learning-based matching for two-stage 
resource management and task offloading archi-
tecture. This method shows improvements in both 
resource management and offloading delays, dem-
onstrating the advantages of adaptive and learning-
based approaches in fog computing.

3  System Model
3.1  Overview
This section describes the proposed task offload-
ing framework in a fog computing environment. The 
framework integrates deep Q-learning (DQL) to opti-
mize offloading decisions dynamically. The system 
consists of multiple fog nodes with varying com-
putational capacities that handle tasks with diverse 
resource requirements. The model ensures efficient 
load balancing and reduced latency through intelli-
gent task distribution.
In our framework, fog computing is chosen over 
edge computing because of its ability to distribute 
computations across multiple nodes rather than rely-
ing on a single edge device. The goal is to optimize 
resource sharing, ensuring that overloaded edge 
devices can offload tasks efficiently. This enables 
dynamic load balancing, improving the overall sys-
tem performance in a fluctuating network environ-
ment. Edge computing is beneficial for localized, 
low-power tasks, but for high-demand applications 
requiring global coordination, fog computing pro-
vides superior scalability, energy efficiency, and load 
distribution.
3.2  Fog Computing Environment
In our model, we have a network of fog nodes, each 
with its own computing power that can change 
depending on workload and node movement. What 
you need to know:
- Fog Nodes: These are the key players in our net-
work. Each node has its own capacity and may face 
delays. Managing these nodes flexibly is crucial since 
their abilities can vary.
- Tasks: Tasks that need processing come with 
specific demands, such as their computational needs, 
size, and deadlines. The challenge is matching these 
tasks to the right nodes on the basis of their current 
workloads and capabilities.

4.3  Task Offloading Model
Building on the MDP and DQL framework, the off-
loading strategy dynamically assigns tasks. The off-
loading strategy, which is given by pseudocode, 
employs the DQL agent to assign tasks dynamically 
to fog nodes by assessing real-time conditions, such 
as the node workload, task computational needs, 
and wireless channel quality. The agent analyzes the 
system state—combining resource availability, task 
demands, and network performance—to choose the 
best node for each task. For example, a task requir-
ing significant processing power and a tight deadline 
is directed to a node with a low current load and a 
reliable connection, ensuring efficient execution. This 
adaptability distinguishes the approach from static 
methods, as it responds to fluctuating conditions such

its strengths in terms of load distribution and queue 
stability, making it an even more versatile solution for 
real-time fog computing environments.
By integrating DQL-based task offloading in fog 
computing, our framework achieves low-latency pro-
cessing, improved load balancing, and reduced energy 
consumption. Future work will explore multiagent 
reinforcement learning techniques to further enhance 
system adaptability. Testing the proposed framework 
in larger, more heterogeneous fog environments and 
under broader dynamic conditions would provide 
valuable insights into its scalability and adaptability. 
Additionally, integrating hybrid AI models that com-
bine reinforcement learning with optimization tech-
niques could increase the task completion time and 
cost efficiency. Finally, applying the framework to 
emerging use cases, such as edge AI for autonomous 
systems and real-time analytics, would validate its 
versatility and practical utility in diverse applications.

Abstract: Fog computing has emerged as a pivotal paradigm for enabling low-latency, high-performance applications by positioning computational resources closer to the network edge. However, task offload- ing in fog environments poses significant challenges because of the dynamic and heterogeneous nature of fog nodes, which are influenced by fluctuating computational loads, channel conditions, and mobil- ity patterns. This paper introduces a dynamic task- offloading framework leveraging deep Q-learning (DQL), a reinforcement learning technique tailored to optimize task allocation and enhance system perfor- mance in such complex settings. The proposed frame- work models the offloading problem as a Markov decision process (MDP), enabling the DQL agent to learn optimal strategies adaptively by incorporating factors such as task demands, node states, and chan- nel quality. Performance evaluations against state-of- the-art scheduling methods reveal that the DQL-based approach consistently outperforms competing tech- niques, achieving superior efficiency and reliability. Furthermore, the framework demonstrates scalabil- ity and robustness in dynamic fog networks, making it highly suitable for diverse real-time applications. This study highlights the potential of DQL as a trans- formative solution for dynamic task offloading in fog computing, offering efficient resource management and system stability. Its applicability to domains such as intelligent transportation systems, smart cities, and the IoT underscores its practical relevance and future impact.
